title: Conejos County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Conejos County wells have a 100 ft median depth and 13.3 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water levels, and buying land.
h1: Water wells in Conejos County, Colorado
intro_html:
In Conejos County, most wells are fairly shallow and produce solid domestic flows, but there’s a wide range once you get into fractured bedrock and the confined San Luis Valley aquifer. Looking at 5,676 permitted wells gives a good picture of what to expect if you own or are buying land near places like La Jara, Manassa, Antonito, Sanford, Romeo, Conejos, or Capulin.

Below is what the county’s well records say about depths, yields, water levels, drilling activity, costs, and the main risks to pay attention to before you drill or close on a property.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Conejos County
sections.html:
Conejos County wells are not especially deep by Colorado standards. The median total depth is about 100 feet, and the middle half of wells run from roughly 50 to 184 feet. About 49% of wells are under 100 feet, another 37% are between 100 and 300 feet, and only 4% go past 600 feet. The deepest well on record reaches 4,000 feet, but that’s an outlier.

For a new domestic well, most drillers here will bid assuming something in that 50–184 foot “middle band,” then price in a contingency in case you hit a tighter fractured-bedrock zone or need to reach the confined San Luis Valley aquifer. Knowing which side of the county you’re on and what nearby wells are doing matters a lot before you budget.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Yields in Conejos County are generally strong for household use. The median reported yield is 13.3 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. That’s plenty for a typical exempt domestic well and small irrigation around a house. About 49% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and another 48% are above 15 gpm.

Only 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 2% land between 1 and 5 gpm, so truly marginal producers are the exception in these records. Still, fractured-bedrock behavior is unpredictable, so two wells a short distance apart can have very different yields. Before you buy acreage around places like Capulin or Conejos, pull the closest well permits to see real-world flows.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they suggest about the aquifer
sections.html:
For wells that report a static water level, the median depth to water is about 25 feet, with the middle half between roughly 10 and 71 feet. That’s a fairly shallow water table, which usually helps with pumping costs and keeps a reasonable buffer between the pump intake and the bottom of the hole.

Looking at median static levels by decade, the numbers sit around 30 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet again in the 2020s. That doesn’t show a clear long-term drop or rise countywide. Conditions still vary between the unnamed fractured-bedrock zones and the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer, so treat this as a general backdrop, not a precise forecast for a single parcel.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how active it’s been
sections.html:
Conejos County has a long well-drilling history. Permit activity jumped in the 1970s with 839 permits, then stayed steady: 447 in the 1980s, 689 in the 1990s, and 1,009 in the 2000s. The 2010s still saw 684 permits, and there are already 467 in the 2020s with records extending through 2026. That tells you the groundwater resource is still being actively developed.

Most permits are for domestic or household use (about 73%), followed by stock wells at 32%, irrigation at 10%, and some monitoring wells. The main aquifer entries are an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer (4,419 wells) and the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer (including 552 wells plus 273 listed as Confined San Luis Valley Aquifer). Common drillers in the records include Heersink Drilling, Valley Pump Company, and Rocky Mountain Waterworks.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Conejos County
sections.html:
The ground here is mostly mixed sedimentary and alluvial material, which tends to drill easier than hard crystalline rock. Typical drilling rates in the county run about $50 to $75 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $5,000 to $7,500.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well commonly lands around $11,000 to $19,500 at that depth. If you’re in an area where nearby wells run closer to the 184-foot upper-middle range, it’s smart to budget off that instead of the median so you’re not surprised by a deeper-than-expected hole.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, contamination, and siting issues
sections.html:
Countywide data shows low-yield wells are relatively rare, but they do exist. With 1% under 1 gpm and another 2% between 1 and 5 gpm, there’s always some chance of a marginal well in fractured bedrock, especially if you’re away from the San Luis Valley aquifer influence. Checking permits around your specific parcel is the best way to gauge that risk.

There are mapped environmental concerns in the broader area: 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. Before drilling or buying, line up your well location with these maps, plan good separation from any existing or future septic system, and be prepared to test new wells for basic potability and, where relevant, site-specific contaminants.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Conejos County
sections.html:
For anyone looking at land near places like La Jara, Manassa, Antonito, Sanford, Romeo, Conejos, or Capulin, start with the neighbors’ wells. Look at their depths, yields, and static levels rather than relying on a countywide average. With 4,088 wells reporting depth and 820 reporting yield, you can usually find a few close analogs.

Confirm the permit type you can get, especially if you plan on stock or irrigation use in addition to household. Think through access for a drill rig, trench routes to the house site, and clear area for a septic system upslope from the well if possible. Bringing this together early makes the difference between a straightforward build and expensive rework once you’re already under contract or in construction.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Conejos County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Conejos County, the median well depth is about 100 feet, with the middle half of wells falling between roughly 50 and 184 feet. About 49% of wells are under 100 feet and another 37% are between 100 and 300 feet. Only 10% go deeper than 300 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet, so truly deep holes are the exception here.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Conejos County?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally good. The median yield is 13.3 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells produce between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. Roughly 49% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range and 48% exceed 15 gpm. Only about 3% of wells report under 5 gpm, which means most domestic wells have comfortable capacity for a home and modest outdoor use.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Conejos County?
faq.a: From the records that include static water level, the overall picture doesn’t show a clear long-term decline. Median depth to water is about 25 feet, with the middle half between roughly 10 and 71 feet. By decade, median levels were around 30 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet again in the 2020s. That suggests short-term fluctuation but no obvious countywide downward trend in the data available.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Conejos County?
faq.a: Typical drilling rates in Conejos County run about $50 to $75 per foot in the local sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone usually runs around $5,000 to $7,500. Once you add casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished domestic well at that depth often totals roughly $11,000 to $19,500, with deeper-than-average wells costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Conejos County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. County records show wells completed in fractured bedrock and the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer, plus some mapped risks nearby: 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. Testing a new or existing well for basic potability and any site-relevant contaminants is important before relying on it for drinking water.
